 6 Analysis 
 To gain insight into when and how context pruning improves long-form dialogue, we analyze three factors. First, we compare GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 to assess how enhanced long-context capabilities in recent LLMs affect the benefits of pruning. We attribute observed shifts in performance to dialogue-level characteristics, such as dialogue length and the position of relevant context (Section  6.1 ). Second, to understand what makes pruning effective, we examine different retrieval configurations, focusing on the trade-off between recall and precision (Section  6.2 ). Third, we investigate whether continuity-preserving turns—those with low but positive relevance—meaningfully contribute to answer quality. To this end, we perform an ablation study that progressively removes the least-relevant turns within the segments selected by DyCP , analyzing how systematically dropping these turns affects downstream performance (Section  6.3 ). All analyses in this section are conducted on the LoCoMo benchmark. 
 6.1 A Study Across GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 
 Figure 6 : 
Win–Tie–Lose breakdown of DyCP compared to Full Context . Each segment represents the proportion of test cases where our method achieved a higher score ( Win ), the same score ( Tie ), or a lower score ( Lose ).
 Figure  6 shows that DyCP achieves better answer quality than Full Context in a larger portion of cases ( Win ) under GPT-4o. However, with GPT-4.1, the two methods produce more similar results, as the proportion of ties increases and the wins decrease. DyCP still offers substantial gains in efficiency, such as fewer input tokens and lower latency (Section  5.5.1 ), but it remains important to understand what accounts for the improved long-context processing observed in GPT-4.1. 
 Figure  7 shows how the number of preceding dialogue turns affects the answer quality in the current turn. Under GPT-4o, Full Context performance drops sharply for long conversations—particularly those exceeding 300 turns—whereas DyCP maintains stable performance even in long conversations. In contrast, GPT-4.1 exhibits no such degradation, with Full Context performing comparably to DyCP across all dialogue lengths. 
 Figure 7 : 
Comparison of answer quality between DyCP and Full Context based on the number of preceding dialogue turns for GPT-4o and GPT-4.1.
 Figure  8 shows the impact of relevant context position on answer quality. Under GPT-4o, Full Context exhibits strong position sensitivity, performing worse when the relevant information appears early in the input (1-100), and gradually improving as it moves closer to the end (301-400). This indicates a recency bias ( Peysakhovich and Lerer, 2023 ; Press et al., 2022 ) , where earlier content is underutilized. With GPT-4.1, position sensitivity largely disappears for Full Context , and its performance becomes comparable to that of DyCP , suggesting improved capacity to retain and attend to long-range information. 
 Figure 8 : 
Comparison of answer quality between DyCP and Full Context based on the relevant context positions for GPT-4o and GPT-4.1.
 When Full Context setting fails under GPT-4o, it typically shows one of two behaviors: (1) hallucinating information or (2) incorrectly claiming that no relevant information is available. Table  9 and Table  10 ( A.1 ) illustrate examples of each case. On the other hand, when Full Context yields better results than DyCP ( Lose ), it is primarily due to imperfect retrievals by DyCP .  6.2 Recall or Precision? 
 To understand what makes pruning effective, we examine how different retrieval configurations influence the trade-off between recall and precision, and how this trade-off, in turn, affects both answer quality and latency. Figure  9 shows the relationship between retrieval recall, precision, and final answer quality across different retrieval configurations in DyCP . We observe a strong positive correlation between recall and answer quality: as recall increases, from Top-1 to Dynamic selection, answer quality steadily improves. This trend suggests that ensuring the inclusion of relevant content (high recall), even at the cost of introducing some mildly irrelevant information (lower precision), is critical for downstream answer generation. However, further increases in recall yield diminishing improvements, indicating that retrieving additional segments beyond a certain point offers limited value. Furthermore, because higher recall typically increases response latency (Figure  10 ), the goal is not simply to maximize recall, but to identify the point at which additional context no longer contributes meaningful gains. 
 Figure 9 : Relationship between retrieval recall, precision, and final answer quality in DyCP . 
 Figure 10 : Relationship between retrieval recall and response latency. 
 These observations also help explain why the concept underlying DyCP ’s dynamic span selection is effective. Unlike fixed top-k approaches, DyCP expands the retrieved span only when the relevance dynamics justify it—adding segments only when sustained positive gain is detected. When relevance drops, the method stops expanding the span, preventing unnecessary context accumulation. This form of adaptive control maintains high recall where it matters while avoiding the latency penalty associated with uniformly larger contexts. In this sense, the concept of DyCP provides a principled mechanism for balancing recall and efficiency in long-form, multi-topic dialogue. 
 6.3 Ablation on Continuity-Preserving Turns 
 To evaluate the contribution of low-relevance but continuity-preserving turns in DyCP , we conduct an ablation study that progressively removes the least-relevant turns from each selected segment while measuring the resulting changes in answer quality and latency. These removed turns correspond to low but positive relevance scores—turns that are not directly needed for answering the current user query but help maintain local continuity and discourse flow within the segment. When removal would leave a segment empty, we retain the single most relevant turn to ensure that each segment preserves at least one anchor point. 
 Figure  11 shows that removing these turns leads to small but consistent drops in answer quality, indicating that even weakly relevant turns contribute useful contextual signals that support downstream generation. Latency decreases slightly as more turns are removed, as expected from the shorter input. Overall, the trend suggests that these low-relevance turns help maintain a more coherent local context, providing modest but meaningful benefits despite their limited direct relevance. 
 Figure 11 : Ablation on continuity-preserving turns. We progressively remove the least-relevant turns within each DyCP -selected segment (Bottom-1/2/3) and compare the resulting answer quality (left axis) and response latency (right axis) against the original Dynamic setting. When removal would leave a segment empty, we retain the single most-relevant turn so that each segment preserves at least one anchor point. 
 7 Discussion 
 We raise the question: "Do LLMs meaningfully process far less context than their actual input token limits?" While models like GPT - 4o support up to 128k tokens, our results indicate that they struggle to fully utilize even 25k tokens, especially when relevant information appears earlier in the input. This observation is consistent with prior findings such as An et al. (2024b) , who show that effective context lengths often fall short, typically not exceeding half of their training lengths. Interestingly, GPT - 4.1, with its 1M token limit, handles the same 25k-token dialogues much more reliably. This contrast suggests that token limits may reflect throughput capacity rather than effective working memory, and that in practice, models may attend to only a smaller, attention-weighted subset of the input. Several factors may contribute to this discrepancy, including the challenge of learning long-range dependencies during training, position-sensitive encoding, and attention saturation. Thus, while token limits continue to grow, effective long-context understanding may remain limited, both due to architectural bottlenecks and practical concerns such as inference cost. 
 8 Conclusion 
 In this work, we present DyCP , a dynamic context pruning method for long-form dialogue that selects query-relevant segments in real time, without pre-segmentation or incurring additional LLM calls. Across three benchmarks, DyCP consistently improves answer quality while significantly reducing response latency. Our findings show that, high recall is more beneficial than precision for retrieval, and preserving the sequential nature of dialogue plays a key role in response generation. We also show that even as LLMs improve in handling longer contexts, context management remains crucial for both response quality and latency. We offer a simple yet effective segment-level context management strategy that is dynamic, scalable, and LLM-agnostic, making it well-suited for real-world deployment. Our research materials, including the source code, the LoCoMo split (Section  5.1 ), and all outputs from each experimental unit (Section  5.5.1 ), are available at: https://github.com/to/be/updated .
